metadata.notes: Framework dictionary for TLCTC v2.5 — the single normative authority for cluster definitions, axioms, and classification rules; all TLCTC documents declare which version of this dictionary they implement. Per-cluster boundary tests are normative but homed in the core paper (§4) by design; this dictionary deliberately carries no boundary_tests field. Lineage: v2.3 consolidated finalized v2.1 content (transit, intra-system, and unresolved-step extensions) with no new normative content vs v2.1. v2.3.1 erratum (2026-07-01): a single axiom-conformance correction — #4 Identity Theft generic_vulnerability retightened from lifecycle/credential-protection wording to the point-of-authentication binding gap, so the field no longer claims scope that R-CRED and Axioms VI/VII/X assign to enabling clusters (storage/transmission/acquisition). Cluster identity and IDs unchanged. v2.3.2 erratum (2026-07-26): a single axiom-conformance correction — #5 Man in the Middle generic_vulnerability retightened from "lack of sufficient control, integrity protection, or confidentiality over the communication channel/path" to "The lack of sufficient control over the communication path", removing consequence-side (confidentiality/integrity) and control-side vocabulary from a cause-side field per Axioms III and V. Cluster identity, IDs, definition, attacker's view, topology, and boundary tests unchanged. v2.4 (2026-07-28): a single clarifying, backward-compatible change on the interaction model — Axiom II restated to remove the network precondition ("All networked systems" → "All system interactions, networked or intra-system"), and R-ROLE extended to state that roles are established by call direction at any interface, including intra-system privilege interfaces (syscall, hypercall, IPC, driver IOCTL), with a cross-reference to R-INTRA-7 so the boundary crossing is not misread as a classification input. No cluster identity, ID, definition, attacker's view, generic_vulnerability, or topology changed; the axiom set is unchanged in count and numbering; no rule was added or removed. Classifications valid under v2.3.2 remain valid under v2.4 — the change resolves an ambiguity rather than altering a decision. Vertical stack analysis (whitepaper §13.5) remains applied guidance and is deliberately NOT part of this dictionary: it introduces no generic vulnerability, axiom, or disambiguation rule and is derivable from Axiom II + R-ROLE + R-INTRA-7 over the 'intra-privilege' boundary context. v2.5 (2026-08-07): two disambiguation rules added — R-CHANNEL and R-SUBSTRATE — completing the family begun by R-FLOOD. Each resolves a weakness describable either as a specific generic vulnerability or as a generic code defect in favour of the specific one, leaving R-ROLE as the residual test. R-CHANNEL: where the defective logic is constitutive of a communication-path control (peer authenticity, channel encryption, algorithm negotiation), the cluster is #5, not #2/#3; R-ROLE governs only where the defect is incidental to the control. R-SUBSTRATE: #8 requires a physical-layer property of the substrate to be the exploited generic vulnerability, and where the physical layer is only the readout channel for a defect in implemented logic the cluster is #2/#3 — attacker proximity or possession is explicitly NOT the test. Rule count 16 → 18; the two are recorded as complementary to the legacy R-PHYSICAL (admission versus sequencing). UNLIKE v2.4, this release is NOT classification-preserving: both rules alter decisions that were defensible under v2.4, and the CWE mapping was re-adjudicated accordingly (certificate/peer-authenticity family → #5; the #8 bucket re-audited from 81 entries to 16, with the remainder resolving to #2, #2 | #3, #2 | #8 or #1 on the property test). No cluster identity, ID, generic_vulnerability, or topology changed; the axiom set is unchanged in count and numbering. Records classified under 2.4 SHOULD be re-checked against R-CHANNEL and R-SUBSTRATE; tlctc-framework.v2.4.json is retained unchanged so those records keep a stable reference. v2.5 pre-publication consistency pass (2026-08-08): #2 and #3 definition and attackers_view retightened from "source code implementation" wording to "implementation flaws within a component acting in a server/client role", making the substrate-neutrality already established by R-ROLE and R-SUBSTRATE explicit in the definitions themselves — implementation flaws in firmware, microcode, or hardware logic classify by component role, resolving the hardware-substrate open question recorded in the CWE mapping notes. Generic_vulnerability fields (already substrate-neutral: "Server-/Client-side implementation flaws enable unintended behavior") unchanged; cluster identity, IDs, and topology unchanged. Rule registry clarified as exactly these 18 rules; v2.0 whitepaper rule IDs R-ABUSE, R-HUMAN, and R-PHYSICAL are retired aliases whose substance is carried by the cluster definitions and boundary tests, and a retired ID is never reused with a different meaning. v2.5 R-CRED clarification (2026-08-14): a single normative clarification to R-CRED (self-issued identity), part of the in-progress v2.5 editing version prior to the first v2.5 Zenodo deposit — v2.5 content, not a post-release erratum. R-CRED's #4 assignment now carries the proviso that credential application is #4 only where the identity claimed is not the presenter's own: a credential issued to the presenter by the target system through a designed enrolment function makes the presenter its authentic holder, so authentication as self exploits no #4 binding gap; where the enrolment function granted the identity or its permissions outside their intended population or scope, that enrolment step maps to #1. This makes explicit in the rule registry the scope the #4 generic_vulnerability already implies ('the authentic holder of the identity it claims') and closes a gap in which an attacker holding a self-enrolled principal was read as #4 by analogy to unauthorized account use. Companion boundary tests added to the core paper §4 (#1 and #4). No cluster identity, ID, definition, attacker's view, generic_vulnerability, or topology changed; the axiom set and rule count (18) are unchanged. UNLIKE the v2.4 clarification, this change is NOT fully classification-preserving: records that classified use of a self-enrolled account as #4 SHOULD be re-checked against the proviso; it joins the v2.5 delta (with R-CHANNEL, R-SUBSTRATE, and the #2/#3 retightening). The canonical-authority declaration was additionally tightened to state that per-cluster boundary tests are normative and homed in the core paper (§4). v2.5 DRE refinement tree (2026-09-05): a new optional data_risk_events section records the Data Risk Event type codes as a refinement tree — C; I with Ii (incorrect state: correspondence/completeness fails) and If (misattributed state: provenance/attribution fails); A with Av (unavailable state) and Ac (inaccessible state) — together with the stopping rule that admits exactly these two splits: a property is split only where the resulting states are distinguishable by inspecting the record itself, never by the story of how it got there. Av/Ac were already v2.5 prose and grammar; Ii/If are new, and they replace the '[DRE: Im]' (manipulated) code proposed for v2.6 in the OpenAI–HF AP-7 path, which fails the stopping rule by naming the actor's intent rather than a record state. Classification-preserving: a parent code stays legal whenever the refinement is unknown or irrelevant, so every existing [DRE: I] and [DRE: A] remains correct; the Layer 3 schema enum and both ABNF grammars now carry all seven codes. No cluster identity, ID, definition, attacker's view, generic_vulnerability, or topology changed; the axiom set and rule count (18) are unchanged. Part of the in-progress v2.5 editing version prior to the first v2.5 Zenodo deposit.

#1.name: Abuse of Functions
#1.definition: An attacker abuses the logic or scope of existing, legitimate software functions for malicious purposes without exploiting a code flaw.
#1.attackers_view: I abuse a functionality, not a coding issue.
#1.generic_vulnerability: The inherent trust, scope, and complexity designed into software functionality and configuration.

#2.name: Exploiting Server
#2.definition: An attacker targets implementation flaws within a component acting in a server role.
#2.attackers_view: I abuse an implementation flaw in a component acting in a server role.
#2.generic_vulnerability: Server-side implementation flaws enable unintended behavior.

#3.name: Exploiting Client
#3.definition: An attacker targets implementation flaws within any component acting in a client role.
#3.attackers_view: I abuse an implementation flaw in a component acting in a client role.
#3.generic_vulnerability: Client-side implementation flaws enable unintended behavior.

#4.name: Identity Theft
#4.definition: An attacker misuses authentication credentials to impersonate an identity.
#4.attackers_view: I abuse stolen or forged credentials to act as someone else.
#4.generic_vulnerability: Insufficient binding, at the point of authentication, between a presented credential and the authentic holder of the identity it claims.

#5.name: Man in the Middle
#5.definition: An attacker intercepts, modifies, or relays communication between two parties by exploiting a privileged position on the communication path.
#5.attackers_view: I abuse my position between communicating parties.
#5.generic_vulnerability: The lack of sufficient control over the communication path.

#6.name: Flooding Attack
#6.definition: An attacker intentionally overwhelms system resources or exceeds capacity limits through a high volume of requests, data, or operations, leading to denial of service.
#6.attackers_view: I abuse the circumstance of always limited capacity.
#6.generic_vulnerability: Finite capacity limitations inherent in any system component.

#7.name: Malware
#7.definition: An attacker abuses the inherent ability of a software environment to execute foreign executable content, including malicious code or legitimate tools executing attacker-controlled code.
#7.attackers_view: I abuse the environment's designed capability to execute malware code, malicious scripts, or foreign-introduced tools for my purposes.
#7.generic_vulnerability: The software environment's designed capability to execute potentially untrusted foreign code.

#8.name: Physical Attack
#8.definition: Unauthorized physical interaction with or interference to hardware, facilities, media, interfaces, or signals—via direct contact or exploitation of physical phenomena/emanations.
#8.attackers_view: I abuse the physical accessibility or properties of hardware, devices, and signals.
#8.generic_vulnerability: Physical accessibility of infrastructure and the exploitability of physical-layer properties.

#9.name: Social Engineering
#9.definition: An attacker psychologically manipulates individuals into performing actions counter to their best interests.
#9.attackers_view: I abuse human trust and psychology.
#9.generic_vulnerability: Humans can be influenced into unsafe actions or decisions.

#10.name: Supply Chain Attack
#10.definition: An attacker compromises systems by targeting vulnerabilities within third-party software, hardware, services, or update mechanisms that are trusted and integrated by the target.
#10.attackers_view: I abuse the trust in third-party components.
#10.generic_vulnerability: Trust in third-party components and update channels can be subverted.

axioms.statement: The framework is generic and applies to all IT systems; it does not differentiate by system type.
All system interactions, networked or intra-system, can be abstracted as client-server interaction.
axioms.notes: v2.4 clarification: a network is not a precondition. A syscall, hypercall, or IPC call establishes the same caller-called relation as a remote protocol exchange, so intra-system privilege interfaces are inside the interaction model. Prior wording ('All networked systems') was read by some implementers as excluding them.

axioms.statement: Threats are on the cause side; outcomes and events are not threats.
Threat clusters are separate from threat actors.
For every generic vulnerability, there is one threat cluster (non-overlap).
Each distinct attack vector is defined by the generic vulnerability it initially targets.
Top-level clusters have sub-threats (strategic vs operational layering).
Clusters can be used in sequence to describe an attack path; Δt measures velocity.
Credentials are system control elements; acquisition and application are distinct steps.

rules.statement: If Foreign Executable Content executes, a #7 step MUST be recorded at the execution moment.

Classify by the role of the component containing the flaw relative to the attacker: server-role flaw = #2, client-role flaw = #3. Roles are established by call direction at any interface, including intra-system privilege interfaces (syscall, hypercall, IPC, driver IOCTL); a network is not a precondition.
rules.notes: v2.4 clarification. A kernel handling a crafted syscall from a lower-privileged process is in server-role for that interaction (#2); a higher-privileged component consuming data or responses returned from a lower-privileged one is in client-role (#3). Per R-INTRA-7 the boundary crossing itself remains an observability annotation and MUST NOT be treated as a classification input — the cluster follows from the role at the interface, exactly as it does across a network.

rules.statement: If the primary mechanism is volume or intensity exhausting finite resources, classify as #6. If it is an implementation defect causing crash/hang/degradation, classify as #2 or #3 per R-ROLE.
#10 Supply Chain Attack MUST be placed at the Trust Acceptance Event (TAE) — the moment the third-party trust link is honored and the trust artifact becomes authoritative inside the target domain.
Position acquisition maps to the enabling cluster; once position is established, interception/modification/relay actions map to #5.

If the defective logic is itself a communication-path control — peer authenticity (certificate validation, chain of trust, hostname matching, expiry or revocation checking), channel encryption, or algorithm negotiation — the generic vulnerability is the lack of sufficient control over the communication path and the weakness classifies as #5, not as #2 or #3 under R-ROLE. R-ROLE governs only where the defect is incidental to the control rather than constitutive of it.
rules.notes: v2.4 addition. R-CHANNEL is the #5 counterpart to R-FLOOD: both resolve the same ambiguity — a weakness describable either as 'a control failed' or as 'the code was wrong' — in favour of the specific generic vulnerability rather than the residual code-flaw test. A missing or incorrect certificate check is not incidentally a code defect; it IS the absence of control over the communication path, which is #5's generic vulnerability (see also the #5 Developer's View, which names certificate/path validation). The rule is constitutive-versus-incidental, not server-versus-client: memory corruption in a TLS parser remains #2/#3 per R-ROLE, because the exploited generic vulnerability there is the code flaw, not the control. R-CHANNEL classifies the weakness; R-MITM sequences the attack path (position acquisition versus action) and is unaffected.

rules.statement: Classify as #8 only where a physical-layer property of the substrate — charge, voltage, electromagnetic emission, temperature, emission-borne timing, wear, or material state — is itself the exploited generic vulnerability. Where the physical layer serves only as the readout channel for a defect in implemented logic, classify by that defect (#2 or #3 per R-ROLE). Attacker proximity or possession is NOT the test: #8 covers exploitation of physical phenomena whether or not the attacker has physical access.
rules.notes: v2.4 addition, completing the family with R-FLOOD (#6) and R-CHANNEL (#5): each resolves a weakness describable either as a specific generic vulnerability or as a generic code defect, in favour of the specific one, with R-ROLE as the residual test. The discriminating question is whether the attack is against the implemented logic or against the physical representation that logic runs on. Rowhammer is #8: charge migration between adjacent DRAM cells IS the vulnerability, no logical control fails, and removing the physics removes the flaw entirely — yet it can be mounted from JavaScript, which is why proximity cannot be the test. Spectre is #2: speculation crosses an isolation boundary the design was meant to enforce, and cache timing is only how the residue is read out — remove the physics and a boundary-crossing design remains. Power side-channel analysis is #8: the cryptography is correct and the emission itself is the vulnerability. Corollary: the location of a flaw — hardware, firmware, silicon — never determines the cluster. Substrate is not cause; per Axiom VI, where foreign code executes to induce the physical effect the execution is a separate #7 step (e.g. #7 → #8). Relationship to the legacy R-PHYSICAL (v2.0 §4.2.5, glossary): the two are complementary and non-conflicting. R-SUBSTRATE is the ADMISSION test — it decides whether a weakness qualifies as #8 at all. R-PHYSICAL is the SEQUENCING rule — given a qualifying physical step, it requires that step to be #8 and subsequent technical steps to be classified separately. R-SUBSTRATE also settles a latent ambiguity in R-PHYSICAL's phrasing ("the attacker's advantage comes from unauthorized physical interaction"), which can be misread as requiring attacker physical access; it does not.

rules.statement: Credential acquisition maps to the enabling cluster. Credential application (use of the credential to authenticate) is ALWAYS classified as #4 Identity Theft, regardless of the acquisition method, PROVIDED the identity claimed is not the presenter's own. A credential issued to the presenter by the target system through a designed enrolment function makes the presenter its authentic holder; such use MUST NOT be classified as #4, and where the enrolment function granted the identity or its permissions outside their intended population or scope, the enrolment step maps to #1. These are separate attack steps.
rules.notes: v2.5 clarification (self-issued identity). Makes normative in the rule registry what the #4 generic_vulnerability already implies ('the authentic holder of the identity it claims'): when the target system itself issued the credential to the presenter, the point-of-authentication binding between presented credential and authentic holder is intact, so authentication as self exploits no #4 generic vulnerability — the exploited generic vulnerability is the scope of the enrolment function and of the permissions attached to the resulting principal (#1). Examples (non-normative): fictitious or pseudonymous self-registration is #1, no identity being impersonated; enrolment completed AS an existing identity (e.g. domain-based auto-affiliation, or identity verification satisfied via prior access to the victim's mailbox) is #1 -> #4 — the enrolment abuse is #1, the subsequent authentication as the victim is #4. NOT fully classification-preserving: records that classified use of a self-enrolled account as #4 SHOULD be re-checked.

rules.statement: Vendor code running on the target device is NOT transit. Software executing on the victim's own device is the attack surface, classified by R-ROLE (typically #3), not a transit (relay/carrier) party.
Intra-system boundary crossings never change cluster classification. They are observability annotations, not classification inputs.
The 'memory' intra-system boundary type is deferred and MUST NOT be used.
'?' and '…' are epistemic annotations, NOT clusters. They have no generic vulnerability, do not appear in cluster definitions, and must not be referenced as if they were '#11'/'#12'.
'?'/'…' are excluded from statistics — they represent absence of knowledge, not a category.
DRE tags ('+ [DRE: ...]') MUST NOT be appended to '?'/'…'. Without a classified cluster there is no causal basis for asserting a data risk event in the notation.
Boundary operators ('||...||', '⇒', '|...|') MAY appear adjacent to '?'/'…' — boundaries are independently observable.
Every '?'/'…' is an open analytical task. Progressively replace with classified steps as evidence matures.
Any path containing '?'/'…' MUST carry a prose annotation explaining what is unresolved and why.
Binary rule: if any cluster can be defended — even weakly — use '#X [conf=low]', not '?'. Reserve '?'/'…' for genuine 'we know something happened, we don't know what' situations.

data_risk_events.description: Data Risk Event (DRE) type codes used in '+ [DRE: ...]' tags. Three parent properties — C (Confidentiality), I (Integrity), A (Availability/Accessibility) — with two admitted refinements: I → Ii/If and A → Av/Ac. A parent code stays legal whenever the refinement is unknown or irrelevant. Codes are outcome annotations recorded on the record that changed state: never clusters, never classification inputs (Axiom III), and never appended to unresolved steps (R-UNRES-5).
data_risk_events.stopping_rule: Split a property only where the resulting states are distinguishable by inspecting the record itself — never by the story of how it got there. The rule admits exactly two splits (I → Ii/If: check provenance and attribution; A → Av/Ac: is the data absent, or present and unusable?), refuses every split of C (accidental versus deliberate disclosure is provenance; one party versus public is extent, i.e. severity, not a state), and refuses any split by cause — outcomes never inherit the classification of the step that produced them (Axiom III).

codes.name: Loss of Confidentiality
codes.definition: Data has been disclosed to a party not entitled to it. No refinement: disclosed data is disclosed, and the record's standing is identical however it leaked.

codes.name: Loss of Integrity
codes.definition: The standing of a record as a faithful and attributable representation has changed other than through its intended, authorised process. Use I when it is unknown or irrelevant whether correspondence (Ii) or provenance (If) failed.

codes.name: Incorrect state
codes.definition: The record no longer corresponds to what it represents, or is no longer complete; read off the record, the content is wrong. Answered by validation, reconciliation and four-eyes controls.

codes.name: Misattributed state
codes.definition: The record claims an origin, author or authority it does not have; read off the record, provenance fails while the content may be perfectly accurate. Answered by segregation of duties, provenance logging and behavioural monitoring.

codes.name: Loss of Availability / Accessibility
codes.definition: Data can no longer serve its intended use by authorised processes. Use A when it is unknown or irrelevant whether the data is gone (Av) or present but unusable (Ac).

codes.name: Unavailable state
codes.definition: Data is gone or unreachable — the resource no longer exists or cannot be technically reached by the infrastructure (deletion, wiper, storage loss, system offline).

codes.name: Inaccessible state
codes.definition: Data is present and reachable but cannot be used for its intended purpose by authorised processes (ransomware encryption, corruption of the container, permission lockout).
